subject: Ch5: Bottom-Up Parsing (Hard)
description: Hard-level MCQs on shift-reduce parsing, handles and viable prefixes, LR(0) items, closure/goto, the LR automaton, SLR/LALR/canonical LR tables, conflicts, and the relative power of the LR family.

questions.text: A handle of a right-sentential form γ is a production A → β and a position where β occurs such that replacing it gives the previous step of a:
options: FIRST-set computation that gathers the leading terminals of every right-hand side
leftmost derivation built by expanding the start symbol downward toward the terminals
rightmost derivation in reverse
regular expression denoting the viable prefixes of the grammar's stack contents
questions.shortExplanation: Handles correspond to reverse-rightmost steps.
questions.explanation: Reducing a handle undoes one step of a rightmost derivation, so bottom-up parsing reconstructs a rightmost derivation in reverse.

questions.text: The set of viable prefixes of a grammar is always a:
options: Finite set whose size is bounded by the number of productions in the grammar
Context-free but non-regular language that no finite-state device can ever recognize correctly
Regular language recognized exactly by the canonical deterministic LR(0) item-set automaton
Context-sensitive language requiring a linear-bounded automaton to recognize its strings
questions.shortExplanation: Viable prefixes form a regular language (the LR automaton).
questions.explanation: Remarkably, the set of viable prefixes is regular and is exactly what the DFA of LR(0) items recognizes, which is why finite-state stacks suffice.

questions.text: CLOSURE of an item set I adds, for each item [A → α • B β] in I and each production B → γ, the item:
options: [A → • α B β], resetting the dot of the enclosing item back to its leftmost position
[B → γ •], the completed item that would instead signal an immediate reduction by B
[A → α B • β], advancing the dot of the original item past the nonterminal B
questions.shortExplanation: Closure adds B's productions with the dot at the start.
questions.explanation: Because the dot precedes nonterminal B, we may begin parsing any B-production, so [B → • γ] is added for every production of B.

questions.text: An LR(0) item [A → α •] (dot at the end) in a state signals a potential:
options: Shift action that consumes the next input terminal and pushes a fresh state
Closure expansion adding more start-dotted items for the nonterminals ahead
Reduce by A → α
Goto on a terminal that advances the automaton without consuming the stack
questions.shortExplanation: A complete item means reduce.
questions.explanation: When the dot reaches the right end, the right-hand side is fully on the stack, indicating a reduction by that production.

questions.text: An SLR(1) parser decides to reduce by A → α in a state only on lookaheads in:
options: FIRST(A), the set of terminals that can begin any string derivable from A
FIRST(α), the set of terminals that can begin the right-hand side α of the rule
the whole alphabet, since SLR reduces unconditionally on every possible input terminal
FOLLOW(A)
questions.shortExplanation: SLR uses FOLLOW(A) to guard reductions.
questions.explanation: SLR adds a reduce action for A → α under each terminal in FOLLOW(A); this coarse criterion is what limits SLR's power.

questions.text: A grammar may be LALR(1) but NOT SLR(1) because LALR uses:
options: FOLLOW sets of the whole grammar, exactly the same coarse criterion that SLR already relies on
more precise per-state (context-specific) lookaheads than FOLLOW, tailored to each item
two lookahead tokens, scanning further ahead in the input than any SLR parser does
no lookahead at all when deciding which completed production to reduce by
questions.shortExplanation: LALR lookaheads are state-specific, finer than FOLLOW.
questions.explanation: LALR computes lookaheads tailored to each item in each state, which can resolve conflicts that SLR's grammar-wide FOLLOW sets cannot.

questions.text: LALR(1) tables are built from canonical LR(1) tables by merging states that have the same:
options: goto entries, collapsing states whose nonterminal transitions lead to identical targets
Lookahead sets, combining any two states whose reduce lookaheads happen to coincide
number of items, regardless of which productions or dot positions those items contain
core (set of LR(0) items ignoring lookaheads), so two canonical LR(1) states with identical item cores are fused and their lookahead sets are unioned together
questions.shortExplanation: Merge LR(1) states with identical cores.
questions.explanation: LALR merges canonical LR(1) states sharing the same core (their items minus lookaheads), unioning the lookaheads, which shrinks the table.

questions.text: Merging cores to form LALR tables can introduce which kind of new conflict (but never the other)?
options: New shift-reduce conflicts but not reduce-reduce, since unioning lookaheads can collide with a shift
Neither kind ever, as core merging is always a perfectly conflict-preserving transformation
New reduce-reduce conflicts but never any shift-reduce ones, as unioned lookaheads can overlap
Both kinds equally, because merging arbitrarily disturbs every action entry in the state
questions.shortExplanation: Core merging can create reduce-reduce, never shift-reduce.
questions.explanation: Merging can union lookaheads so two reductions collide (reduce-reduce), but it cannot create a shift-reduce conflict that LR(1) lacked.

questions.text: The augmented production S' → S exists so that the parser can perform the ACCEPT action when it is about to reduce by:
options: an ε-production, because an empty reduction on the end-marker is what terminates the parse
the first production listed in the grammar specification supplied to the parser generator
any production whatsoever, since reaching a complete item on the end-marker always means accept
S' → S with the lookahead $, i.e. the end-of-input marker is the only lookahead under which this augmenting reduction is taken and reported as accept
questions.shortExplanation: Accept = reduce S' → S on $.
questions.explanation: Reducing the augmenting production with the end-marker as lookahead is treated specially as the accept action, signaling successful parse.

questions.text: The GOTO function of the LR automaton, GOTO(I, X), is defined for X being:
options: nonterminals only, while terminals use shift
either a terminal or a nonterminal (the goto table column is for nonterminals)
the end-marker only, since GOTO is consulted just once at the very end of the parse
terminals only, because GOTO models the shift transitions taken on input symbols
questions.shortExplanation: GOTO table is for nonterminals; terminals drive shifts.
questions.explanation: Conceptually GOTO(I,X) moves the dot over X; in the parsing table, transitions on terminals are shift entries in ACTION while transitions on nonterminals fill GOTO.

questions.text: Which ordering correctly ranks the grammar classes by inclusion (subset → superset)?
options: SLR(1) ⊆ LALR(1) ⊆ LR(1)
LR(1) ⊆ SLR(1) ⊆ LALR(1), ranking canonical LR below both SLR and LALR parsers
LR(1) ⊆ LALR(1) ⊆ SLR(1), making SLR the most powerful and canonical LR the weakest
LALR(1) ⊆ SLR(1) ⊆ LR(1), placing SLR strictly above LALR in expressive power
questions.shortExplanation: SLR ⊆ LALR ⊆ canonical LR(1).
questions.explanation: Every SLR(1) grammar is LALR(1), and every LALR(1) grammar is LR(1); the inclusions are proper, reflecting increasing power.

questions.text: A shift-reduce conflict in an LR(0) state means the state contains BOTH:
options: two complete items only, each with its dot already at the very end of a right-hand side
a complete item [A → α •] and an item with the dot before a terminal [B → β • a γ]
two items with the dot at the start, both freshly added by the closure operation
no items at all, leaving the parser unable to decide between shifting and reducing
questions.shortExplanation: Reduce item plus a shiftable terminal item = shift-reduce.
questions.explanation: If a state can reduce (complete item) and also shift a terminal (dot before that terminal), the parser faces a shift-reduce conflict on that terminal.

questions.text: Operator-precedence parsing handles ambiguous expression grammars by:
options: using precedence relations (⋖, ≐, ⋗) between terminals to locate handles, bracketing each handle between a ⋖ marking its left end and a ⋗ marking its right end during the parse
rewriting them to LL(1) form by eliminating left recursion and left-factoring the rules
computing FIRST and FOLLOW only, then driving the parse from those two sets alone
ignoring associativity entirely and reducing operators strictly from left to right
questions.shortExplanation: Precedence relations between terminals find handles.
questions.explanation: Operator-precedence parsers use the relations ⋖, ≐, ⋗ among terminals to bracket the handle, parsing operator grammars even when ambiguous.

questions.text: Why are LR parsers able to handle left-recursive grammars naturally?
options: They forbid recursion and force the writer to remove every recursive rule
They shift input and reduce handles, making progress regardless of recursion side
They convert recursion to iteration in the scanner so the parser never sees recursive rules
They expand nonterminals top-down, predicting each production before any input is consumed
questions.shortExplanation: Shift-reduce makes input progress, so recursion side is irrelevant.
questions.explanation: Bottom-up parsing consumes input via shifts and reduces handles as they complete, so left recursion (even preferred for LR) causes no looping.

questions.text: In an LR(1) item [A → α • β, a], the lookahead 'a' is used:
options: only when the dot reaches the end, to decide whether to reduce A → αβ
to compute FIRST of the part already to the left of the dot
to decide a shift on α, choosing whether to push α's symbols onto the parsing stack
to label the start state of the canonical LR(1) automaton built for the augmented grammar
questions.shortExplanation: Lookahead guards the eventual reduction.
questions.explanation: The lookahead component constrains the reduce action: A → αβ is reduced only when the next input symbol is the item's lookahead 'a'.

questions.text: A reduce-reduce conflict occurs in a state that contains:
options: only goto entries that move the automaton across nonterminals
two distinct complete items [A → α •] and [B → γ •] reducible on a common lookahead
one complete item and one shift item whose dot still sits before an upcoming terminal
no complete items, so the state offers nothing but shift and goto transitions to take
questions.shortExplanation: Two completed productions valid on the same lookahead.
questions.explanation: When two different productions are both fully recognized and both applicable on the same lookahead, the parser cannot choose — a reduce-reduce conflict.

questions.text: The stack of an LR parser actually stores states (not just symbols) because:
options: the state on top encodes the viable prefix, telling the parser which action/goto to take
it avoids using a parsing table altogether, running with no ACTION or GOTO
states are faster to print when the parser dumps a trace of its moves for debugging purposes
symbols are unnecessary, since the grammar's terminals can be inferred from the input buffer alone
questions.shortExplanation: Top state summarizes the viable prefix for table lookup.
questions.explanation: Each stacked state represents the LR automaton's position after the symbols seen, so the top state directly indexes ACTION/GOTO.

questions.text: Which statement about LR(0) parsing is TRUE?
options: It is more powerful than SLR(1), accepting strictly more grammars than the FOLLOW-based method
It uses one lookahead token to guard each reduction, exactly as an SLR(1) parser does
It reduces whenever a state has a complete item, regardless of lookahead, so any shift-reduce overlap is a conflict
It never has conflicts because LR(0) states are guaranteed to mix neither shifts nor reduces
questions.shortExplanation: LR(0) reduces with no lookahead → easy conflicts.
questions.explanation: LR(0) takes a reduce action on a complete item without consulting lookahead, so it conflicts whenever a state mixes shift and reduce (SLR adds FOLLOW to help).

questions.text: For S → C C, C → c C | d, the canonical LR(1) and LALR(1) tables differ in size but for THIS grammar LALR introduces:
options: left recursion in the production for C, turning the right-recursive rule into a left-recursive one
ambiguity, so that two distinct rightmost derivations exist for some input string of c's and d's
no new conflicts (it remains conflict-free), since the same-core canonical states for this grammar carry compatible lookaheads that union without any reduce-reduce clash
new shift-reduce conflicts that the canonical LR(1) construction for this grammar did not have
questions.shortExplanation: This classic grammar is LALR(1) with no new conflicts.
questions.explanation: The standard S → CC, C → cC | d example merges cores cleanly; LALR yields fewer states than canonical LR(1) without creating conflicts.

questions.text: A YACC/Bison default resolution applies precedence/associativity declarations to resolve a shift-reduce conflict; without them it:
options: halts the build immediately and refuses to emit any parser until the conflict is removed
shifts by default and warns about the conflict, resolving every shift-reduce clash in favor of the shift action and emitting a diagnostic count of such conflicts
chooses randomly at run time, picking shift or reduce differently on each separate parse
reduces by default, always favoring the reduce action over the competing shift in the state
questions.shortExplanation: Default: shift over reduce, with a warning.
questions.explanation: Absent precedence directives, YACC favors shift for shift-reduce conflicts (and the earlier rule for reduce-reduce), emitting a diagnostic.

questions.text: The number of states in the LR(0)/SLR automaton versus the canonical LR(1) automaton is typically:
options: fewer for LR(0)/SLR; canonical LR(1) often has many more states
always exactly double, with every LR(0) state splitting into precisely two canonical LR(1) states
fewer for canonical LR(1), since carrying lookaheads lets several LR(0) states be merged into one
the same, since lookaheads never split any LR(0) state
questions.shortExplanation: Canonical LR(1) splits states by lookahead → more states.
questions.explanation: Carrying lookaheads splits states, so canonical LR(1) usually has many more states; LALR collapses them back to the LR(0) core count.

questions.text: Which is a viable prefix of the right-sentential form for E → E + T | T, T → id, when parsing 'id + id'?
options: id id, two adjacent identifiers that never appear consecutively in any right-sentential form
E +
E + T id, which already extends past the completed handle and so cannot sit on the stack
+ T, beginning with an operator that no right-sentential form of this grammar starts with
questions.shortExplanation: 'E +' is a prefix not extending past a handle.
questions.explanation: 'E +' is a prefix of a right-sentential form (E + T) that stops before completing the handle, so it can legally sit on the stack — a viable prefix.

questions.text: The ACTION table entry 'sj' (shift to state j) is placed for state i on terminal a when GOTO(Iᵢ, a) =:
options: Iⱼ (there is a transition on terminal a to state j)
the empty set, meaning there is no transition on a out of state i and the cell stays blank
a reduce item, signalling that the parser should reduce rather than shift on the terminal a
the start state, redirecting the parser back to the initial item set whenever a is read in
questions.shortExplanation: Shift entry mirrors a terminal transition in the automaton.
questions.explanation: If moving the dot over terminal a leads from state i to state j, the parser shifts a and goes to state j, recorded as ACTION[i,a]=shift j.

questions.text: Handle pruning, viewed on the stack, means a handle always appears:
options: on top of the stack when it is ready to be reduced
split across the stack and input, with part already shifted and part still to be read
only in the input buffer, never on the stack, until the entire input has been consumed
at the bottom of the stack, beneath every other symbol that the parser has so far shifted
questions.shortExplanation: Handles surface at the stack top for reduction.
questions.explanation: A key property of shift-reduce parsing is that the handle is always found at the top of the stack, never buried, enabling simple reductions.

questions.text: Which grammar feature most directly causes a grammar to be LR(1) but not LALR(1)?
options: two same-core LR(1) states whose unioned lookahead sets create a new reduce-reduce conflict
an ε-production, since empty right-hand sides cannot be represented inside any LALR state
operator precedence declarations that override the lookaheads computed for the merged states
left recursion in some production, which always defeats the LALR core-merging construction
questions.shortExplanation: Core-merge-induced reduce-reduce breaks LALR.
questions.explanation: LR(1)-but-not-LALR(1) grammars are exactly those where merging same-core states unions lookaheads into a reduce-reduce clash.

questions.text: In bottom-up parsing, a 'shift' move:
options: outputs a production number to the derivation trace without touching the stack at all
pushes the next input terminal (and a state) onto the stack, advancing the input pointer by one symbol so that the recognized prefix on the stack grows by that terminal
pops the stack down to the last accepting state recorded during the current parse
replaces the top handle with the nonterminal on the left-hand side of its matching production
questions.shortExplanation: Shift pushes the next input symbol/state.
questions.explanation: A shift moves the current input terminal onto the stack along with the resulting LR state, advancing the input pointer.

questions.text: Why is the set of LR(0) items called the 'canonical collection'?
options: It is picked arbitrarily by the implementer from many valid collections
It is the smallest possible set of states among all automata that recognize the same language
It contains only complete items with dots at the right end
It is the unique set of item sets generated by closure and goto from the augmented start item
questions.shortExplanation: Unique closure/goto-generated collection of item sets.
questions.explanation: Starting from CLOSURE({S' → •S}) and repeatedly applying GOTO yields a unique (canonical) collection of LR(0) item sets — the automaton's states.

questions.text: A complete item [A → α •] together with FOLLOW(A) = {a, b} causes an SLR parser to place reduce actions under:
options: no column at all, leaving the reduce action for A → α entirely absent from this state's row
FIRST(α) only, the set of terminals that can begin the right-hand side α of the rule
every terminal, so the parser reduces by A → α no matter which input symbol it is currently facing
columns a and b, placing the reduce-by-A action in exactly those two ACTION cells of this state because they are precisely the terminals in FOLLOW(A)
questions.shortExplanation: Reduce under FOLLOW(A) = {a,b}.
questions.explanation: SLR adds 'reduce A → α' in the ACTION row of that state for each terminal in FOLLOW(A), here a and b.

questions.text: If a grammar is ambiguous, its LR parsing table will:
options: always be conflict-free, since the LR construction silently resolves every ambiguity on its own
have no reduce actions at all, leaving only shift and goto transitions throughout the table
be impossible to construct at all, so the parser generator cannot even begin building it
contain at least one conflict (a multiply-defined ACTION entry) unless resolved by added rules
questions.shortExplanation: Ambiguity ⇒ table conflicts (need disambiguation).
questions.explanation: Ambiguous grammars produce multiply-defined ACTION entries; tools handle them via precedence/associativity rules rather than rejecting outright.

questions.text: The fundamental advantage of LR parsing over LL parsing is that LR parsers:
options: use less memory always, needing a strictly smaller table than any LL parser
require ambiguous grammars and cannot operate on grammars that have a single unique parse tree
produce leftmost derivations directly, emitting each production as a nonterminal expands
postpone the decision about which production to use until the entire right-hand side is seen
questions.shortExplanation: LR decides after seeing the whole handle.
questions.explanation: By delaying the production decision until a complete handle is on the stack, LR parsers recognize a strictly larger class of grammars than LL parsers.
